title: Bits: Reverse Bits of a 32-bit Unsigned Integer
oneLiner: Mirror all 32 bits: pop the lowest bit of n, push it onto the result from the right, exactly 32 times.
keyTakeaway: result = (result << 1) | (n & 1), then n >>= 1, repeated exactly 32 times, not "until n is 0" (leading zeros become trailing zeros and still count). Use an unsigned type in C# (uint) so >> shifts in zeros; in Python, ints have no width, so the fixed loop count is what makes it 32-bit.
explanation:
Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer: bit 0 swaps with bit 31, bit 1 with bit 30, and so on. Unsigned means all 32 bits are value bits, so the range is 0 to 4,294,967,295 and there are no negative numbers. 1 (only bit 0 set) becomes 2,147,483,648 (only bit 31 set), and 43,261,596 becomes 964,176,192.

The loop treats n as a stack of bits. n & 1 reads the lowest bit. n >> 1 shifts every bit one place to the right, dropping that bit. result << 1 shifts the result left to make room, and | (OR) drops the new bit into the empty lowest place. So each round moves one bit from the bottom of n to the bottom of result, and after 32 rounds the first bit taken (n's bit 0) has been pushed all the way up to bit 31. Run exactly 32 rounds: if you stop when n becomes 0, the zeros at the top of n never get moved to the bottom, and 1 would come out as 1 instead of 2,147,483,648.

Signed versus unsigned shifts. In C#, >> on a signed int is an arithmetic shift: it copies the sign bit into the top, so a negative number stays negative and never reaches 0. On a uint, >> is a logical shift that fills with zeros, which is why this lesson's C# signature takes and returns uint. C# 11 also added >>>, a logical right shift for signed types. Python has no >>> and no fixed width: >> on a negative int is arithmetic, and a left shift just makes the number bigger. Here the input is non-negative, so Python's >> is fine, and the 32-round loop is what keeps the result 32 bits wide.

If the function is called many times, cache the reversal of every byte (256 entries) and combine four lookups; or swap halves, then quarters, with masks like 0xFFFF0000, 0xFF00FF00, 0xF0F0F0F0, 0xCCCCCCCC and 0xAAAAAAAA, five steps with no loop.

The visualization reverses an 8-bit number, 0b00001101 (13), so it fits on screen; the real thing is the same loop with 32 rounds.

The input is described as unsigned or as a fixed-width bit string.

gotchas: Loop exactly 32 times; stopping when n == 0 loses the bits that should become trailing zeros.
In C#, use uint (or >>>): >> on a negative int copies the sign bit and the value never empties.
Shift result left BEFORE OR-ing in the new bit, or the last bit gets shifted one place too far.

complexity.note: Always exactly 32 rounds, whatever the value: constant time for a fixed-width integer.

referenceSolutions.python:
def reverse_bits(n):
    result = 0
    # Exactly 32 rounds: Python ints have no width, so the loop count is what fixes it at 32 bits.
    for _ in range(32):
        result = (result << 1) | (n & 1)  # push n's lowest bit onto result
        n >>= 1
    return result
